messages.subject: Problem using Particle Filter in simple SI model
messages.subject_clean: Problem using Particle Filter in simple SI model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was hoping to use PMCMC on a more complicated compartmental SIR model. After a number of setbacks, I decided to start from the simple and use particle filter to evaluate a simple SI model (Susceptible -> Infected).

Here's my code:
library(nimble)
library(nimbleSMC)

#### Model
SI <- nimbleCode({
  S[1] <- iniState[1]
  I[1] <- iniState[2]
  y[1] ~ dpois(pdet * I[1] + 1e-5)
  for (t in 2:nT) {
    lambda[t] <- beta * I[t-1] / N * S[t-1] + 1e-5
    negdS[t] ~ dpois(lambda[t])

    S[t] <- S[t-1] - negdS[t]
    I[t] <- I[t-1] + negdS[t]

    y[t] ~ dpois(pdet * I[t] + 1e-5)
    X[1:2,t] <- c(S[t], I[t])
  }

  beta ~ dunif(0, 0.3) #Transimissibility
  pdet ~ dunif(0, 1) #Probability of detection
})

states <- c(10000, 5)
constants <- list(
  N = sum(states),
  nT = 50,
  iniState = states
)

y <- c(0, 3, 2, 2, 8, 9, 3, 6, 7, 5, 6, 10, 14, 9, 8, 16,
       15, 20, 27, 29, 37, 33, 32, 52, 55, 67, 56, 68, 85, 85, 111,
       124, 145, 169, 206, 203, 260, 277, 320, 335, 414, 438, 539, 621,
       681, 783, 932, 1015, 1099, 1222)

SIMod <- nimbleModel(code = SI,
                     constants = constants,
                     data = list(y = y),
                     inits = list(beta = 0.2, pdet = 0.5))

my_AuxF <- buildAuxiliaryFilter(SIMod, 'I',
                                control = list(saveAll = TRUE))
SIModC <- compileNimble(SIMod)
my_AuxFC <- compileNimble(my_AuxF, project = SIMod)
logLik <- my_AuxFC$run(m = 10000)
logLik # Always -Inf

The code runs and my nimble model should work since I could simulate data using SIMod$simulate() and the simulated dataset looks correct. However, the log-likelihood evaluated by the algorithm is always -Inf. I am not sure if it was my model's problem, or my code's problem. I have tried using Bootstrap filter instead, and I have swapped out the Poisson distribution with Normal and I still get -Inf log-likelihood. Might anyone know what could have been the problem here?

Thank you!

Cheers,
Ben

On Thu, 31 Dec 2020 at 20:40, Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
>
> Fraser, it looks like you're already on the right track.  I'll just re-mention, that Chris's first suggestion ("Rewrite the names in the model such that y[39300,1:3] is not part of 'y', but has its own variable name") is a really dead-simple and easy way to go.  Implementing that strategy would look like:
>
> code <- nimbleCode({
>     .....
>     yPred[1:3] <- y[39300,1:3]    ## add this line to your model code
> })
>
> Then, when you add MCMC monitors (mcmcConf$addMonitors), don't add any monitors to any parts of "y", and instead:
>
> mcmcConf$addMonitors(..., "yPred")
>
> That's all you'd need to do.  This approach has the added cost of adding 3 more nodes (actually only 1 node, a length-3 vector) to your model, which is not a large overhead when compared to everything else going on.  And it has the advantage of simplicity.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>
>
>
>
> On Thu, Dec 31, 2020 at 9:04 AM fraser lewis <fraser.i...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> >
>> > predictorNF <- nimbleFunction(
>> >   setup = function(model, input_nodes, output_nodes) {
>> >      update_nodes <- model$getDependencies(input_nodes)
>> >      length_output_nodes <- length(model$expandNodeNames(output_nodes, returnScalarComponents=TRUE))
>> >   },
>> >   run = function(MCMCmatrix = double(2)) {
>> >     m <- dim(MCMCmatrix)[1] # number of saved MCMC iterations
>> >     outputMatrix <- matrix(nrow = m, ncol = length_output_nodes)
>> >     for(i in 1:m) {
>> >        values(model, input_nodes) <<- MCMCmatrix[i,] # You'll need to be sure the order of input_nodes matches the column order of MCMCmatrix
>> >        model$calculate(update_nodes) # update anything that depends on input_nodes
>> >        model$simulate(output_nodes) # insert "includeData = TRUE" if you need to simulate new values into data nodes
>> >        outputMatrix[i, ] <- values(model, output_nodes)

>> >     }
>> >   }

>> >>>
>> >>> inits <- list(beta0 = rep(0.1,3), beta1 = rep(0.1,13),beta2 = rep(0.4,13),beta3 = rep(0.5,13), beta21=0.1,beta31=0.2, beta32=0.2,

messages.subject: Re: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.subject_clean: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

You shouldn't need to have any knowledge of nimble's under-the-hood operations for runCrossValidate to be able to set up the foldFunction and lossFunction input functions - our hope is that the help information on runCrossValidate() is sufficient. Namely that the foldFunction should return a character vector of (data) node names and the lossFunction a function that takes in two vectors and computes the loss.

 If you'd like us to delve into this further, it would be helpful to have a (as simple as possible) reproducible example where things go wrong for you.

-Chris

On Thu, Dec 31, 2020 at 9:59 AM Andrew <ajden...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Chris,
>
> Thanks for the feedback.
>
> Regarding the NAs, yeah, it's mostly about adding user convenience to runCrossValidate( ), especially in light of observational studies. You're absolutely right that loss cannot be computed from non-data; that certainly wasn't my ask, and I apologize if my previous messages were somewhat unclear.
>
> Following your suggestions from a couple of weeks ago, I attempted to code fold functions that would "ignore" or "skip over" NAs in the dependent variables, but each of those attempts were unsuccessful, which is likely due to my lack of complete understanding of NIMBLE's under-the-hood operations for runCrossValidate( ). For example, it wasn't clear to me how I could exclude NAs in either my fold function or in the simulatedDataValues or actualDataValues within my loss function. Instead, I decided to take a simpler approach and just leave out the NAs entirely by removing the 6th replicates in both seasons a priori, limiting model validation to an extent. Recall that NAs only occurred in my dependent variables during (missing) 6th replicate surveys in the first season.
>
> About the syntax errors, I really don't know what went wrong, but it's no longer a problem after a re-run. I didn't make any changes to the input code (e.g., because I did not see any comma, parenthesis, or bracket problems), and no errors were ultimately thrown. I have no idea what occurred the first time. If you'd still like to see a reproducible, then I would be happy to forward you one off-list.
>
> Best,
> Andrew
>
> On Thursday, December 31, 2020 at 11:35:07 AM UTC-5 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > hi Andrew,
> >
> > Regarding handling of NAs, I'd need more information on what your goal is in order to be able to respond usefully. Given one can't use an NA to calculate a loss, it's not clear to me what it means to include values with NAs in a held-out set. Do you just want nimble to be able to handle this for convenience - i.e., that nodes with NAs could be included in a fold but would be ignored? If so, that's something we could probably do quite easily, though the development team would have to discuss if it's something we want as part of the user interface.
> >
> > Regarding your syntax errors, those indeed look odd. Would you be able to share a minimal reproducible example (off-list if you prefer) so I can look in more detail?
> >

> > On Wed, Dec 30, 2020 at 10:54 AM Andrew <ajden...@gmail.com> wrote:

Do you also have an update on what the Development Team suggests for running cross-validation on models with datasets containing NAs in the dependent variable(s)?
> > >
> > > On a different note, for a dynamic N-occupancy model (i.e. including sub-models for occupancy and abundance and associated measurement errors for y_occ ~ dbern(psi) and y_abund ~ dbin(N, p) input dependent data), is runCrossValidate( ) able to generate performance scores from a loss function on two processes, both occupancy and abundance? > > >
> > > To do so, I have been experimenting with the following code:
> > > #Cross-validate model results
> > > commNocc_FoldFunction <- function(i){

> > >   ##foldNodes_i <- c(paste0('Yc_occ[', i,', , , ]'), paste0('Yc_abund[', i,', , , ]'))  # changing the order because the measurement error process for Yc_abund appears first in modelCode
> > >   return(foldNodes_i)
> > > }
> > >
> > > # The function below computes the root mean squared error
> > > RMSE_lossFunction <- function(simulatedDataValues, actualDataValues){
> > >   dataLength <- length(simulatedDataValues) # simulatedDataValues is a vector
> > >   SSE <- 0

> > >     SSE <- SSE + (simulatedDataValues[i] - actualDataValues[i])^2
> > >   }

> > >

> > > #####################################################
> > >
> > > model <- nimbleModel(code = modelCode, name = "modelCode",
> > >                      constants = const, data = win.data,
> > >                      inits = init)
> > > Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

> > >
> > > cvSamples <- runCrossValidate(MCMCconfiguration = modelConf,
> > >                                k = 5, foldFunction = commNocc_FoldFunction,
> > >                                lossFunction = RMSE_lossFunction,
> > >                                MCMCcontrol = list(niter = ni, nburnin = nb))

> > > ###

> > > Do these error messages indicate that runCrossValidate( ) cannot handle models with more than one dependent variable, or is my syntax for the foldFunction incorrect?
> > > On Thursday, December 10, 2020 at 6:21:59 PM UTC-5 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Yes, using an if statement to handle the special case should work, or any other R code that serves to omit the nodes that are not observed but would otherwise be included for any given value of "i".
> > > >
> > > > As I'm looking at this, it appears there might be a use for having the fold function take an optional additional argument (via R's ... functionality) that could be used to determine which nodes are valid data nodes. I'll bring this up with the development team.
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, Dec 10, 2020 at 11:53 AM Andrew <ajden...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Thanks for responding, Chris. Your reply confirms my suspicion: the NA records do inhibit the cross-validation. Conceptually, I understand what you recommend to do as a workaround, but I must admit that I do not know how to accurately implement such recommendations in practice.
> > > > >
> > > > > The NA records are stored in the dependent variable at Yc[1:14, 1:26, 1, 6], for 1-14 sites, 1-26 species, season 1, and the missing 6th replicate.
> > > > >
> > > > > How could I adapt my foldFunction to accommodate skipping over such records? Could if/then loops be used somehow?
> > > > >
> > > > > commNmix_FoldFunction <- function(i){

> > > > >   return(foldNodes_i)

> > > > > Before receiving your response today, I had considered simply inserting 0's for NAs during the first season, but that then inserts invalid ecological information into the process. I had also considered cross-validating the model over 1-5 replicate records only, but that then leaves out quite a bit of information from the 6th replicate visits recorded during season 2. > > > > > On Thursday, December 10, 2020 at 11:32:31 AM UTC-5 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > hi Andrew,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > We don't consider missing observations to be data nodes (because they don't contribute to the likelihood and in an MCMC are treated as 'parameters' in the sense that they are sampled during the MCMC).
> > > > > > Furthermore, we can't use those nodes for cross-validation because the values are unknown. So you'd need to have your fold function avoid specifying any nodes that are missing data nodes as part of the fold.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > -Chris
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Tue, Dec 8, 2020 at 11:15 AM Andrew <ajden...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > Hello,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > runCrossValidate( ) is throwing me an error that I suspect results from missing data in the dependent variable of a dynamic multi-species occupancy model. In the dataset, only 5 of 6 possible replicate survey visits were conducted by technicians during the first season of data collection, whereas the second season contains data for all 6 replicate visits. Therefore, the missing 6th replicate contains NAs for all sites and species in the first season. The dependent variable, called Yc, is indexed by site, species, season, and replicate, respectively.

messages.body_plain:
hi Andrew,

Regarding the question of multiple RMSE values, I don't think it's directly possible to return multiple RMSE values for each fold as we've set things up to expect that the lossFunction returns a scalar. However, if within each fold, the first "m" values in each vector input to the lossFunction correspond to counts and the remaining values correspond to presence/absence and "m" is the same for each fold, you could presumably have the lossFunction set up to combine the two component losses and return the overall loss for each fold. Does that make sense?

And if you really want them separate you could presumably run runCrossValidate()  twice, the first time where the hold-out is over occupancy data nodes and the second time where the hold-out is over abundance data nodes. That would involve two separate MCMC runs, one each time runCrossValidate is called.

-chris

Namely that the foldFunction should return a character vector of (data) node names and the lossFunction a function that takes in two vectors and computes the loss.

For example, it wasn't clear to me how I could exclude NAs in either my fold function or in the simulatedDataValues or actualDataValues within my loss function. messages.body_plain:
Thank you for these additional recommendations, Chris. I don't think there's a need for the development team to dive further into the first issue (i.e. working fold and loss functions around non-data nodes). For simplicity, I will compute loss over the first 5 (rather than all 6) replicates of the input datasets.

Replying to your second message, the first suggestion is a bit challenging to follow. In the current model version, my occupancy inputs (i.e. with their indices) belong to an array called Yc_occ[ site, species, season, replicate ]; whereas abundance inputs (i.e. with their indices) belong to an array called Yc_abund[ site, species, season, replicate ]. Their dimensions are thus equivalent: 14 sites, 26 species, 2 seasons, and 5 replicates (i.e. when ignoring the 6th, which is missing during season 1). Would those input dimensions work with your first suggestion?

If not, then I could certainly run runCrossValidate( ) twice, along with their requisite MCMCs. In that regard, is it permissible to hold out a portion of the occupancy inputs, but not the abundance inputs simultaneously? In other words, should the following work to retrieve separate RMSEs:
#Cross-validate model results
occupancy_FoldFunction <- function(i){
  foldNodes_i <- paste0('Yc_occ[', i,', , , ]')  # will return 'y[1,,,]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)  return(foldNodes_i)
}

abundance_FoldFunction <- function(i){
  foldNodes_i <- paste0('Yc_abund[', i,', , , ]')  # will return 'y[1,,,]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)  return(foldNodes_i)
}

# The function below computes the root mean squared error
RMSE_lossFunction <- function(simulatedDataValues, actualDataValues){

  dataLength <- length(simulatedDataValues) # simulatedDataValues is a vector
  SSE <- 0
  for(i in 1:dataLength){
    SSE <- SSE + (simulatedDataValues[i] - actualDataValues[i])^2
  }
  MSE <- SSE / dataLength
  RMSE <- sqrt(MSE)
  return(RMSE)
}

######### Here is where I exclude the 6th replicate surveys#########
win.data$Yc_abund <- win.data$Yc_abund[,,,1:5]
win.data$Yc_occ <- win.data$Yc_occ[,,,1:5]
const$nrep <- dim(win.data$Yc_abund)[[4]]
#####################################################

model <- nimbleModel(code = modelCode, name = "modelCode",
                     constants = const, data = win.data,
                     inits = init)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)

cvSamples_occ  <- runCrossValidate(MCMCconfiguration = modelConf,
                               k = 5, foldFunction =  occupancy_FoldFunction   ,

                               lossFunction = RMSE_lossFunction,
                               MCMCcontrol = list(niter = ni, nburnin = nb))

cvSamples_abund <- runCrossValidate(MCMCconfiguration = modelConf,
                               k = 5, foldFunction =  abundance_FoldFunction   ,
                               lossFunction = RMSE_lossFunction,

                               MCMCcontrol = list(niter = ni, nburnin = nb))

###

Based on your second suggestion, it seems as though holding out a portion of one of the dependent inputs (e.g., occupancy) and not the other (e.g., abundance) would not generate MCMC estimation problems for runCrossValidate( ).

messages.subject: Re: Problem using Particle Filter in simple SI model
messages.subject_clean: Problem using Particle Filter in simple SI model
messages.body_plain:
hi Ben,

It looks like the -Inf is coming from numerical underflow in our calculations of weights in the particle filtering algorithm. This occurs for this specific model (and not others on which we've used nimble's particle filters) because of the large counts in the Poisson likelihood (producing very small likelihood values) as well as because the structure of the model induces many dependent data nodes for each latent node (resulting in a sum of many large magnitude negative log-likelihoods). That said, the underlying issue is that our numerical approach for working with the weights and log-likelihood values could be much more robust. Thanks for posting your question so that we are able to recognize this issue.

We'll try to make it a priority to work on this in the next couple weeks and at least get a branch on our GitHub repository that addresses the issue (making a release would take a bit longer).

Side note: in your call to buildAuxiliaryFilter, the 'nodes' argument should be 'negdS', since that is the variable containing the latent **stochastic** nodes.

-chris

messages.subject: Re: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.subject_clean: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.body_plain:
hi Andrew,

The fold function says which nodes to hold out for a given fold and the values of those nodes are concatenated and passed along to the loss function. The key is making sure that your loss function knows which of the elements it receives are for occupancy and which for abundance so it can calculate the loss appropriately for those two pieces and combine the two values together. So based on what nodes your fold function is returning, you need to know how many of the values correspond to occupancy and how many to abundance and which of the values are for occupancy and which for abundance. Given the symmetry you seem to have, it might be as simple as the first half of the nodes are occupancy and the second half are abundance and so the loss function does one thing with the first half of the values and something else with the second half of the values.

Regarding my suggestion to run runCrossValidate twice, I may have been a bit hasty with that suggestion. If you hold out only, say, occupancy, then the corresponding abundance is not held out and does inform the parameters. That may not be what you want.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Chris. That makes a lot more sense to me now, and I was not previously aware that runCrossValidate( ) concatenates data from multiple nodes when they're simultaneously held out with a fold function. My datasets are, indeed, very congruent, and so I will begin testing whether I can use the first and second halves in different ways within my loss function or not. My first thought is to specify both hold outs in the fold function (i.e. occupancy and abundance, in that order) and then divide dataLength, simulatedDataValues, and actualDataValues in half, computing the occupancy and abundance RMSEs, respectively. Please let me know if that doesn't accurately follow your suggestion.

On your last note, that was my concern as well. I assumed that it would be the case that holding out one without the other would be incorrect, but it's also very helpful to hear your thoughts on the matter, helping validate my intuition.

Andrew

On Tuesday, January 5, 2021 at 12:01:31 PM UTC-5 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> hi Andrew,
>
> The fold function says which nodes to hold out for a given fold and the values of those nodes are concatenated and passed along to the loss function. The key is making sure that your loss function knows which of the elements it receives are for occupancy and which for abundance so it can calculate the loss appropriately for those two pieces and combine the two values together. So based on what nodes your fold function is returning, you need to know how many of the values correspond to occupancy and how many to abundance and which of the values are for occupancy and which for abundance. Given the symmetry you seem to have, it might be as simple as the first half of the nodes are occupancy and the second half are abundance and so the loss function does one thing with the first half of the values and something else with the second half of the values.
>
> Regarding my suggestion to run runCrossValidate twice, I may have been a bit hasty with that suggestion. If you hold out only, say, occupancy, then the corresponding abundance is not held out and does inform the parameters. That may not be what you want.
>
> -chris

messages.body_plain:
Great; that also sounds like an excellent approach. I'll give that a shot. Thanks again, Chris. I really appreciate your time discussing this problem with me.

On Tue, Jan 5, 2021 at 2:27 PM Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Yes, what you say follows my thoughts.
>
> One other thought on a possibly useful hack here. If for some reason you wanted to hold out both occupancy and abundance together but be able to report the loss separately for occupancy and abundance, your loss function could ignore either the occupancy or abundance values, just returning the loss for one of them. You could then run runCrossValidate twice - once with a loss function that computes the occupancy+abundundance loss and once with a loss function that computes, say, only the loss for occupancy. Then you'd have in your hands the total loss and the two component pieces. Note that the fold function would still be set up to hold out the relevant occupancy and abundance values together. I haven't looked at how the random number seeds are being set in all of this - you'd want the two calls to runCrossValidate to produce the exact same MCMC output.
>
> -chris
>

> On Tue, Jan 5, 2021 at 9:35 AM Andrew <ajden...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Thanks, Chris. That makes a lot more sense to me now, and I was not previously aware that runCrossValidate( ) concatenates data from multiple nodes when they're simultaneously held out with a fold function. My datasets are, indeed, very congruent, and so I will begin testing whether I can use the first and second halves in different ways within my loss function or not. My first thought is to specify both hold outs in the fold function (i.e. occupancy and abundance, in that order) and then divide dataLength, simulatedDataValues, and actualDataValues in half, computing the occupancy and abundance RMSEs, respectively. Please let me know if that doesn't accurately follow your suggestion.
> >
> > On your last note, that was my concern as well. I assumed that it would be the case that holding out one without the other would be incorrect, but it's also very helpful to hear your thoughts on the matter, helping validate my intuition.
> >
> > Andrew
> >
> > On Tuesday, January 5, 2021 at 12:01:31 PM UTC-5 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > hi Andrew,
> > >
> > > The fold function says which nodes to hold out for a given fold and the values of those nodes are concatenated and passed along to the loss function. The key is making sure that your loss function knows which of the elements it receives are for occupancy and which for abundance so it can calculate the loss appropriately for those two pieces and combine the two values together. So based on what nodes your fold function is returning, you need to know how many of the values correspond to occupancy and how many to abundance and which of the values are for occupancy and which for abundance. Given the symmetry you seem to have, it might be as simple as the first half of the nodes are occupancy and the second half are abundance and so the loss function does one thing with the first half of the values and something else with the second half of the values.
> > >
> > > Regarding my suggestion to run runCrossValidate twice, I may have been a bit hasty with that suggestion. If you hold out only, say, occupancy, then the corresponding abundance is not held out and does inform the parameters. That may not be what you want.
> > >
> > > -chris
> > >
> > > On Mon, Jan 4, 2021 at 9:48 AM Andrew <ajden...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thank you for these additional recommendations, Chris. I don't think there's a need for the development team to dive further into the first issue (i.e. working fold and loss functions around non-data nodes). For simplicity, I will compute loss over the first 5 (rather than all 6) replicates of the input datasets.
> > > >
> > > > Replying to your second message, the first suggestion is a bit challenging to follow. In the current model version, my occupancy inputs (i.e. with their indices) belong to an array called Yc_occ[ site, species, season, replicate ]; whereas abundance inputs (i.e. with their indices) belong to an array called Yc_abund[ site, species, season, replicate ]. Their dimensions are thus equivalent: 14 sites, 26 species, 2 seasons, and 5 replicates (i.e. when ignoring the 6th, which is missing during season 1). Would those input dimensions work with your first suggestion?
> > > >
> > > > If not, then I could certainly run runCrossValidate( ) twice, along with their requisite MCMCs. In that regard, is it permissible to hold out a portion of the occupancy inputs, but not the abundance inputs simultaneously? In other words, should the following work to retrieve separate RMSEs:
> > > > #Cross-validate model results
> > > > occupancy_FoldFunction <- function(i){
> > > >   foldNodes_i <- paste0('Yc_occ[', i,', , , ]')  # will return 'y[1,,,]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)  return(foldNodes_i)
> > > > }
> > > >

> > > >   foldNodes_i <- paste0('Yc_abund[', i,', , , ]')  # will return 'y[1,,,]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)  return(foldNodes_i)
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > # The function below computes the root mean squared error
> > > > RMSE_lossFunction <- function(simulatedDataValues, actualDataValues){
> > > >   dataLength <- length(simulatedDataValues) # simulatedDataValues is a vector
> > > >   SSE <- 0
> > > >   for(i in 1:dataLength){
> > > >     SSE <- SSE + (simulatedDataValues[i] - actualDataValues[i])^2
> > > >   }
> > > >   MSE <- SSE / dataLength
> > > >   RMSE <- sqrt(MSE)
> > > >   return(RMSE)
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > ######### Here is where I exclude the 6th replicate surveys#########

> > > > win.data$Yc_occ <- win.data$Yc_occ[,,,1:5]
> > > > const$nrep <- dim(win.data$Yc_abund)[[4]]
> > > > #####################################################
> > > >
> > > > model <- nimbleModel(code = modelCode, name = "modelCode",
> > > >                      constants = const, data = win.data,
> > > >                      inits = init)
> > > > Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> > > > modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> > > >
> > > > cvSamples_occ  <- runCrossValidate(MCMCconfiguration = modelConf,
> > > >                                k = 5, foldFunction =  occupancy_FoldFunction   ,
> > > >                                lossFunction = RMSE_lossFunction,
> > > >                                MCMCcontrol = list(niter = ni, nburnin = nb))
> > > >

> > > >                                lossFunction = RMSE_lossFunction,
> > > >                                MCMCcontrol = list(niter = ni, nburnin = nb))
> > > >
> > > > ###
> > > >
> > > > Based on your second suggestion, it seems as though holding out a portion of one of the dependent inputs (e.g., occupancy) and not the other (e.g., abundance) would not generate MCMC estimation problems for runCrossValidate( ).
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, January 4, 2021 at 12:25:53 PM UTC-5 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > hi Andrew,
> > > > >
> > > > > Regarding the question of multiple RMSE values, I don't think it's directly possible to return multiple RMSE values for each fold as we've set things up to expect that the lossFunction returns a scalar. However, if within each fold, the first "m" values in each vector input to the lossFunction correspond to counts and the remaining values correspond to presence/absence and "m" is the same for each fold, you could presumably have the lossFunction set up to combine the two component losses and return the overall loss for each fold. messages.subject: NAs in the linear predictor
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I hope I find you well. I have simulated some data to do some checks before running my main model. The model is pretty straight forward, it have just a covariate. What is cumbersome with my problem is the dataset which is fairly large (approx 400,000 rows).

I wrote the code and decided to store the linear predictor (which of course makes the result very large). Say mu is the linear predictor, I observed that for mu[100000], mu[200000], mu[300000] and mu[400000] the first element of the chain is NA and the rest are zeros, which I find extremely weird.

Please find my code and dataset attached (its extremely simple as an example). Note also that it took me approx 3 hours to run it. Any ideas?

findata.linear <- readRDS("dat")

linear_Code <- nimbleCode(
  {
    for (i in 1:N){

      O[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
      log(mu[i]) <- log(E[i]) + alpha + beta_1*lag0[i]

    }

    # Priors:
    alpha ~ dflat()
    exp.alpha <- exp(alpha)

    beta_1 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    exp.beta_1 <- exp(beta_1)
  }
)

# Format the data for NIMBLE in a list
tempData = list(
  O = as.numeric(findata.linear$`1`)
)

tempConsts <-list(
  N = nrow(findata.linear),
  lag0 = findata.linear$meanTemp,
  E = findata.linear$expected
)

params <- c("alpha", "mu", "beta_1")

# MCMC setting
ni <- 50000  # nb iterations
nt <- 10     # thinning interval
nb <- 10000  # nb iterations as burn-in

inits <- list(
  alpha=0.01,
  beta_1=0
)

t_0 <- Sys.time()

model <- nimbleModel(linear_Code, constants = tempConsts, data = tempData, inits = inits)
cModel <- compileNimble(model)

conf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = params)

MCMC <- buildMCMC(conf)
cMCMC <- compileNimble(MCMC, project = cModel)

linear_Model <- runMCMC(cMCMC, niter = ni, nburnin = nb, thin = nt)

t_1 <- Sys.time()
t_1 - t_0

tmp <-
apply(linear_Model, 2, FUN = function(X) sum(is.na <http://is.na>(X)))
which(tmp != 0) - 2

You can download the data from hear:

https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/100zyipZgfo1o6u7Dv7_dhfBgz4vO5Sen?usp=sharing

Best wishes,
Gary

messages.body_plain:
Gary, I've given your code a go.  I'm not sure what's different, but I don't seem to be experiencing the same issue that you did.  The exact code that I ran is below, including a small amount of the MCMC output at the end.  At least in my run, I'm not seeing the NA's, or the 0's that you mentioned.

The only changes I made were:

- Adding the argument "calculate = FALSE" to the nmbleModel() function, to speed it up heaps.
- Adding a call to cModel$calculate(), to verify that the model is in a valid initial state - which it is.
- Adding set.seed(0) right before the call to runMCMC(), for reproducibility.
- Reducing the number of MCMC iterations to 100, and removing the burnin and thinning intervals.

In the MCMC output at the end, we can see real numbers being generated for the parameters and also for elements of mu, and also a few transitions taking place (although not yet in beta_1) in the parameter values.  So it seems to be working OK to me, and I'm not sure what the difference is.  Otherwise, I'm stumped on why your MCMC output was different.  Maybe someone else will have an idea, or can weigh in.

Cheers, keep in touch, and good luck,
Daniel

library(nimble)

findata.linear <- readRDS("~/Downloads/dat")

linear_Code <- nimbleCode({

    alpha ~ dflat()
    exp.alpha <- exp(alpha)
    beta_1 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    exp.beta_1 <- exp(beta_1)

    for (i in 1:N){
        O[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

thanks a lot for your prompt reply :)

I was able to reproduce your outcome and now I do not have NAs. Nevertheless, I tried a couple of things too and I observed that the behaviour i describe above is when you remove calculate = FALSE from the nimbleModel(). For instance if you run the code you attached removing calculate = FALSE you will see that the first element of the chain of mu[100000], mu[200000], mu[300000] and mu[400000] is NA and the rest are 0s.

This is a bit weird right? Do you have any explanation?

Best wishes,
Gary

messages.body_plain:
Gary, I'll continue looking into this, and see if I can reproduce the problem you're describing.  But in the meantime, I'm glad to hear that adding "calculate = FALSE" fixes the problem for you.

On Sat, Jan 9, 2021 at 12:47 PM Konstantinoudis Akis <g.konsta...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Daniel,
>
> thanks a lot for your prompt reply :)
>
> I was able to reproduce your outcome and now I do not have NAs. Nevertheless, I tried a couple of things too and I observed that the behaviour i describe above is when you remove calculate = FALSE from the nimbleModel(). For instance if you run the code you attached removing calculate = FALSE you will see that the first element of the chain of mu[100000], mu[200000], mu[300000] and mu[400000] is NA and the rest are 0s.
>
> This is a bit weird right? Do you have any explanation?
>
> Best wishes,
> Gary

> > The only changes I made were:
> >
> > - Adding the argument "calculate = FALSE" to the nmbleModel() function, to speed it up heaps.
> > - Adding a call to cModel$calculate(), to verify that the model is in a valid initial state - which it is.
> > - Adding set.seed(0) right before the call to runMCMC(), for reproducibility.
> > - Reducing the number of MCMC iterations to 100, and removing the burnin and thinning intervals.
> >
> > In the MCMC output at the end, we can see real numbers being generated for the parameters and also for elements of mu, and also a few transitions taking place (although not yet in beta_1) in the parameter values. messages.subject_clean: Problem using Particle Filter in simple SI model
messages.body_plain:
hi Ben,

I've reworked the numerical approach to avoid the underflow problem in a branch on our GitHub repository. That should address the problem you were facing, so please feel free to try again after installing the updated version from the branch:

remotes::install_github("https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleSMC", ref = "fix_underflow", subdir = "packages/nimbleSMC")

We'll get this into a release of nimbleSMC in coming weeks.

-chris

On Mon, Jan 4, 2021 at 10:52 AM Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> hi Ben,
>
> It looks like the -Inf is coming from numerical underflow in our calculations of weights in the particle filtering algorithm. This occurs for this specific model (and not others on which we've used nimble's particle filters) because of the large counts in the Poisson likelihood (producing very small likelihood values) as well as because the structure of the model induces many dependent data nodes for each latent node (resulting in a sum of many large magnitude negative log-likelihoods). That said, the underlying issue is that our numerical approach for working with the weights and log-likelihood values could be much more robust. Thanks for posting your question so that we are able to recognize this issue.
>
> We'll try to make it a priority to work on this in the next couple weeks and at least get a branch on our GitHub repository that addresses the issue (making a release would take a bit longer).
>
> Side note: in your call to buildAuxiliaryFilter, the 'nodes' argument should be 'negdS', since that is the variable containing the latent **stochastic** nodes.
>
> -chris
>
> On Thu, Dec 31, 2020 at 11:40 PM Kok Ben Toh <kok...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I was hoping to use PMCMC on a more complicated compartmental SIR model. After a number of setbacks, I decided to start from the simple and use particle filter to evaluate a simple SI model (Susceptible -> Infected).
> >
> > Here's my code:
> > library(nimble)
> > library(nimbleSMC)
> >
> > #### Model
> > SI <- nimbleCode({
> >   S[1] <- iniState[1]
> >   I[1] <- iniState[2]
> >   y[1] ~ dpois(pdet * I[1] + 1e-5)
> >   for (t in 2:nT) {
> >     lambda[t] <- beta * I[t-1] / N * S[t-1] + 1e-5
> >     negdS[t] ~ dpois(lambda[t])
> >
> >     S[t] <- S[t-1] - negdS[t]
> >     I[t] <- I[t-1] + negdS[t]
> >
> >     y[t] ~ dpois(pdet * I[t] + 1e-5)
> >     X[1:2,t] <- c(S[t], I[t])
> >   }
> >
> >   beta ~ dunif(0, 0.3) #Transimissibility
> >   pdet ~ dunif(0, 1) #Probability of detection
> > })
> >
> > states <- c(10000, 5)
> > constants <- list(
> >   N = sum(states),
> >   nT = 50,
> >   iniState = states
> > )
> >
> > y <- c(0, 3, 2, 2, 8, 9, 3, 6, 7, 5, 6, 10, 14, 9, 8, 16,
> >        15, 20, 27, 29, 37, 33, 32, 52, 55, 67, 56, 68, 85, 85, 111,
> >        124, 145, 169, 206, 203, 260, 277, 320, 335, 414, 438, 539, 621,
> >        681, 783, 932, 1015, 1099, 1222)
> >
> > SIMod <- nimbleModel(code = SI,
> >                      constants = constants,
> >                      data = list(y = y),
> >                      inits = list(beta = 0.2, pdet = 0.5))
> >
> > my_AuxF <- buildAuxiliaryFilter(SIMod, 'I',
> >                                 control = list(saveAll = TRUE))
> > SIModC <- compileNimble(SIMod)
> > my_AuxFC <- compileNimble(my_AuxF, project = SIMod)
> > logLik <- my_AuxFC$run(m = 10000)
> > logLik # Always -Inf
> >
> > The code runs and my nimble model should work since I could simulate data using SIMod$simulate() and the simulated dataset looks correct. However, the log-likelihood evaluated by the algorithm is always -Inf. I am not sure if it was my model's problem, or my code's problem. I have tried using Bootstrap filter instead, and I have swapped out the Poisson distribution with Normal and I still get -Inf log-likelihood. Might anyone know what could have been the problem here?
> >
> > Thank you!
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Ben
> >

Hi all,

I am VERY new to nimble and currently trying to convert my multivariate state-space model in jags to nimble code and I'm running into what is probably rudimentary issues.

I am trying to set the priors on the first timestep of each population's (location) state vector within an array.

for ( l in 1:Nloc){

X[1,1,l] ~dnorm(1,5)

}

where Nloc equals the number of states, which in this case represents populations from different locations. X will ultimately be an array of matrices, where each matrix has the dimensions of Nyears by 1, representing the population state vector through time.

The code above outputs the error:

Error in array(as.numeric(NA), dim = varInfo[[iV]]$maxs) :
  negative length vectors are not allowed
In addition: Warning message:
In array(as.numeric(NA), dim = varInfo[[iV]]$maxs) :
  NAs introduced by coercion

I have tried to set the dimensions of X in the nimbleModel with no luck. Might anyone know what could be the issue and any solutions? I've come across nimbleFunctions as a solution, but would appreciate some direction.

Thanks,
Jordan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

Thanks for getting back to me so quickly. Here is the nimble code. After some tinkering I realize that the error code most likely stems from the observation model later in the model (highlighted in yellow). Here is the full model:

nc <- nimbleCode({
  #---------------
  # DEFINE PRIORS
  #---------------

  ## Prior for step parameter (U parameter in MARSS models)
  #--------------------------------------------------------

  for (l in 1:Nloc){

    step[l] ~ dunif(-10,10) # time-invariant

  }

  ## Prior for Q parameter (Process error MARSS models)
  #--------------------------------------------------------

  # Q prior from wishart distribution: dwish ~ (omega, degrees of freedom)

  tauQ[1:Nloc, 1:Nloc] ~ dwish(Omega[1:Nloc,1:Nloc], Nloc)

  for (l in 1:Nloc) {

    Omega[l,l] <- l

  }

  for (i in 1:(Nloc-1)) {
    for (j in (i+1):Nloc) {

      Omega[i,j] <- 0
      Omega[j,i] <- 0

    }
  }

  # MVN Process error

  sigmaQ[1:Nloc, 1:Nloc] <- inverse(tauQ[1:Nloc, 1:Nloc]) # convert from precision to sd

  ## Prior for R parameter (observation error in MARRS model)
  #----------------------------------------------------------

  # Assuming observation error is different for each location

  for(l in 1:Nloc) {

    tauR[l] ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001)
    sigmaR[l] <- 1/sqrt(tauR[l])

  }

  ## MVN prior on initial state for each location
  #---------------------------------------------

  for (l in 1:Nloc){

    X[1,1,l] ~dnorm(1,5)

  }

  ## Priors for thresholds
  #------------------------

  for(l in 1:Nloc){

    tau[l,1] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)

    for(j in 1:3){

      delta[l,j] ~ dexp(2)
      tau[l,j+1] <- tau[l,j] + delta[l,j]

    }
  }

  ## Prior for random efect of location
  #---------------------------------

  for (l in 1:Nloc){

    loc.eta[l] ~ dnorm(loc.muhat,loc.tau)

  }

  loc.muhat ~ dunif(-10,10)
  loc.tau <- 1/pow(loc.sigma,2) ## convert stddev to precision (sigma defiend above)
  loc.sigma ~ dunif(0,5)

  ## Prior for random efect of site
  #---------------------------------

  for (s in 1:Nsite){

    site.eta[s] ~ dnorm(site.muhat,site.tau)

  }

  site.muhat ~ dunif(-10,10)
  site.tau <- 1/pow(site.sigma,2) ## convert stddev to precision (sigma defiend above)
  site.sigma ~ dunif(0,5)

  ## Prior for random effect of diver
  #-----------------------------------

  for (k in 1:Ndiver){

    diver.eta[k] ~ dnorm(diver.muhat,diver.tau)

  }

  diver.muhat ~ dunif(-10,10)
  diver.tau <- 1/pow(diver.sigma,2) ## convert stddev to precision (sigma defiend above)
  diver.sigma ~ dunif(0,5)

  #-------------------
  # OBSERVATION MODEL
  #-------------------

  for (l in 1:Nloc){

      #cumulative logistic probabilities

  #-------------------

Hi,

I'm quite new to nimble, but have tried to fit a few models and nimble really sped up computation time (a lot), so thank you!

Now I've run into an error that I don't understand when compiling:

Hi Daniel,

Thanks for your quick reply! I can't spot anything where I'm looping over node names but I might be wrong. Here's my (almost unabridged) code:

totalT <- 5
theta_init <- c(0.3, 0.95, 0.9, 2.0e-04, 8, 120)
phi_p_init <- theta_init[1]
phi_a_init <- theta_init[2]
alpha_init <- theta_init[3]
beta_init <- theta_init[4]
rho_init <- theta_init[5]
tau_init <- theta_init[6]
y0 <- 500
y <-  c(668,649,834,747,903)

code <- nimbleCode({
  ##### Priors
  phi_p ~ dbeta(2.87, 1.78)
  phi_a ~ dbeta(1.6, 1.2)
  alpha ~ dbeta(2, 1.5)
  beta ~ dgamma(2, 1/(3.7e-04/2))
  rho ~ dgamma(4, 1/2.5)
  tau ~ dgamma(2.1, 1/66.67)
  ##### Initialisation
  x_upd[, ] <- matrix(nrow = totalT+1, ncol = 2)
  x_pred[, ] <- matrix(nrow = totalT, ncol = 2)

  x0[1:2] <- y0*c(1, 1/alpha)
  sigma2 <- y0^2/tau
  P011 <- sigma2
  P022 <- 1/(alpha^2)*((1-alpha)*y0+sigma2)
  P012 <- 1/alpha*sigma2
  P021 <- 1/alpha*sigma2
  T12 <- alpha*phi_a
  T22 <- phi_a
  x_upd[1, 1:2] <- x0[1:2]
  P_upd11[1] <- P011
  P_upd12[1] <- P012
  P_upd21[1] <- P021
  P_upd22[1] <- P022
  for(t in 1:totalT){
    real_phi_p[t] <- phi_p/(1+(beta*x_upd[t, 1])^rho)
    T21[t] <- 0.5*real_phi_p[t]
    T11[t] <-  alpha*0.5*real_phi_p[t]
    Q11[t] <- alpha*(1-alpha)*(0.5*real_phi_p[t]*x_upd[t, 1]+phi_a*x_upd[t, 2])
    Q22[t] <- 0.5*real_phi_p[t]*(1-0.5*real_phi_p[t])*x_upd[t, 1] + phi_a*(1-phi_a)*x_upd[t, 2]
    Q12[t] <- alpha*(0.5*real_phi_p[t]*(1-0.5*real_phi_p[t])*x_upd[t, 1] + phi_a*(1-phi_a)*x_upd[t, 2])
    Q21[t] <- alpha*(0.5*real_phi_p[t]*(1-0.5*real_phi_p[t])*x_upd[t, 1] + phi_a*(1-phi_a)*x_upd[t, 2])
    R_matrix[t] <- x_upd[t, 1]^2/tau
    # Prediction
    x_pred[t, 1] <- T11[t]*x_upd[t, 1] + T12*x_upd[t, 2]
    x_pred[t, 2] <- T21[t]*x_upd[t, 1] + T22*x_upd[t, 2]
    P_pred11[t] <- (T11[t]*P_upd11[t]+T12*P_upd21[t])*T11[t]+(T11[t]*P_upd12[t]+T12*P_upd22[t])*T12+Q11[t]
    P_pred12[t] <- (T11[t]*P_upd11[t]+T12*P_upd21[t])*T21[t]+(T11[t]*P_upd12[t]+T12*P_upd22[t])*T22+Q12[t]
    P_pred21[t] <- (T21[t]*P_upd11[t]+T22*P_upd21[t])*T11[t]+(T21[t]*P_upd12[t]+T22*P_upd22[t])*T12+Q21[t]
    P_pred22[t] <- (T21[t]*P_upd11[t]+T22*P_upd21[t])*T21[t]+(T21[t]*P_upd12[t]+T22*P_upd22[t])*T22+Q22[t]
    # Aid variables
    y_pred[t] <- x_pred[t, 1]
    v_pred[t] <- y[t] - y_pred[t]
    F_matrix[t] <-P_pred11[t] + R_matrix[t]
    G1[t] <- P_pred11[t]
    G2[t] <- P_pred21[t]
    F_inv[t] <- F_matrix[t]^(-1)
    K1[t] <- G1[t]*F_inv[t]
    K2[t] <- G2[t]*F_inv[t]
    # Distribution of y
    y[t] ~ dnorm(y_pred[t], var = F_matrix[t])
    # Update
    x_upd[t+1, 1] <- x_pred[t, 1] + K1[t]*v_pred[t]
    x_upd[t+1, 2] <- x_pred[t, 2] + K2[t]*v_pred[t]
    P_upd11[t+1] <- P_pred11[t] - F_inv[t]*G1[t]^2
    P_upd12[t+1] <- P_pred12[t] - F_inv[t]*G1[t]*G2[t]
    P_upd21[t+1] <- P_pred21[t] - F_inv[t]*G1[t]*G2[t]
    P_upd22[t+1] <- P_pred22[t] - F_inv[t]*G2[t]^2
  }
})

mNimble_seal2 <- nimbleModel(code,
                             dimensions = list(x_upd = c(totalT+1,2),
                                               x_pred = c(totalT,2)),
                             data = list(y=y, y0 = y0),
                             constants = list(totalT = totalT),
                             inits = list(phi_p = phi_p_init,
                                          phi_a = phi_a_init,
                                          alpha = alpha_init,
                                          beta = beta_init,
                                          rho = rho_init,
                                          tau = tau_init),
                             check = FALSE)

compNimble_seal2 <- compileNimble(mNimble_seal2)
confNimble_seal2 <- configureMCMC(mNimble_seal2,
                                  print = TRUE, useConjugacy = FALSE)

mcmcNimble_seal2 <- buildMCMC(confNimble_seal2)

# This runs but slowly
# fNimble_seal2 <- runMCMC(mcmcNimble_seal2,
#                          nburnin = 10,
#                          nchains = 2,
#                          niter = 110)

# This is where the error happens
mcmccNimble_seal2 <- compileNimble(mcmcNimble_seal2,
                                   project = mNimble_seal2,
                                   resetFunctions = TRUE,
                                   showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Fanny, the issue is the inclusion of the matrix() declaration lines in your model code.  These are not necessary, and in fact are causing an issue down the line.  You should *not* include these two lines:

    x_upd[, ] <- matrix(nrow = totalT+1, ncol = 2)
    x_pred[, ] <- matrix(nrow = totalT, ncol = 2)

More troublesome, from the package development perspective, is how/why this slipped through model checking.  This should have been caught at the time of model building, and ideally issue a helpful message to correct the problem.

We'll look into that, improving the error-catching for this case, but for right now this should get your model and MCMC running.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: User-defined prob 'd' function without 'r' function
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
I would like to implement some bespoke (non-standard) user-defined density functions but as I have not created an 'r' function (only a 'd' function) I get the error

'Error: In sizeAssignAfterRecursing: 'rmynorm' is not available or its output type is unknown".

Looking at the manual it seems to imply that an 'r' function is not necessary (see https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-user-defined.html#fn22). This is important as I have a set of non-standard densities without any easy way to simulate from them (and I was hoping the samplers in nimble would take care of this?).   If there some setting I could adjust to help? e.g. choose a specific sampler?

thanks for your help!
Fraser

## some example code - it's a simple polynomial regression
library(nimble, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

dmynorm <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = double(0), mu = double(0, default = 0),sigma = double(0, default = 1),
        log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
        returnType(double(0))
        logProb <- (1/2)*( -((mu - x)^2/sigma^2) - log(2*pi) - 2*log(sigma) )
        if(log) return(logProb)
        else return(exp(logProb))
    })

code <- nimbleCode({

  sigma ~ dunif(0, 1000)
  a0 ~ dmynorm(0,sigma=1000)
  a1 ~ dmynorm(0,sigma=1000)
  a2 ~ dmynorm(0,sigma=1000)

  for(i in 1:n) {
    Observation[i] ~ dnorm(mean = a0+a1*Time[i]+a2*Time[i]*Time[i], sd=sigma)
    }

})

constants <- list(n = nrow(data1))
data <- list(Observation = data1$Observation)
inits <- list(a0=0.1, sigma = 1)
model <- nimbleModel(code, constants = constants, data = data1, inits = inits) # build model
myMCMCconf <- configureMCMC(model)
myMCMC<-buildMCMC(myMCMCconf)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model,resetFunctions = TRUE)
CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(myMCMC, project = Cmodel,resetFunctions = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Fraser, you are correct, that NIMBLE should auto-generate this "random generation" function for you, in this case, the function called "rmynorm".  At one point, this functionality was a "new" addition to NIMBLE, although I feel like a few years ago now, it's been a while.  What version of NIMLBE are you using?  Perhaps try installing the most recent release 0.10.1, from CRAN?

Anyway, on my system, after adding the line below to have the data1 data frame:

data1 <- data.frame(Observation = 1:5)   ## added this line

your exact code runs fine, with the warning:

> model <- nimbleModel(code, constants = constants, data = data1, inits = inits) # build model

defining model...
Registering the following user-provided distributions: dmynorm
Warning: random generation function for dmynorm is not available. NIMBLE is generating a placeholder function, rmynorm, that will invoke an error if an algorithm needs to simulate from this distribution. Some algorithms (such as random-walk Metropolis MCMC sampling) will work without the ability to simulate from the distribution.  If simulation is needed, provide a nimbleFunction (with no setup code) to do it.

So I'm not sure what the hang-up is.  That said, if you really can't get it working, implementing a placeholder "rmynorm" function is straightforward, and should get around the problem you're having, just by adding this definition.  This will never be called by the MCMC, and if it were, it will issue an error.

rmynorm <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(n = integer(0), mu = double(0, default = 0),sigma = double(0, default = 1)) {
        stop('rmynorm should never be run')
        returnType(double(0))
        return(0)
    })

Hope this helps,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Yes, sorry I didn't notice the lack of initial values before.  Let me explain quickly.

Basically, you didn't provide initial values for "a1" or "a2" in the "inits" list.  Before the MCMC gets going, the model object needs to be in a valid starting position - with all stochastic nodes in the model having valid values.  Afterall, the MCMC needs to start off from somewhere, right?  Since you didn't provide initial values for "a1" or "a2", the model initialization routine does what it thinks is a good idea to generate those - it calls the (in this case) rmynorm() function, to draw values for each of them from their prior distributions.  However, in this case, we (fortunately) protected against this unintentional use of that function, by putting that error message in the rmynorm() function, since yours won't actually be implemented.

Anyway, that's a long-winded explanation for saying - just provide value initial values for "a1" and "a2", and the model checking / initialization that takes place *won't* need to generate values for them (since valid values already exist in the model), and therefore *won't* try calling the rmynorm function.  A line like:

inits <- list(a0=0.1, a1=0.1, a2=0.1, sigma = 1)

Should do it just fine.

Cheers, keep at it,
Daniel

A self contained example is below. In the model below I do have a data likelihood and it still gives the error about no 'r' function.

Any suggestions welcome! thanks. Fraser.

library(nimble, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
sessionInfo()

926.84000000000003,
 794.17999999999995, 784.40999999999997, 748.5, 1008.22, 1202.47,
 1290.3699999999999)), row.names = 301:315, class = "data.frame")

dsde <- nimbleFunction(

    run = function(x = double(0),

                   X0 = double(0, default = 0),
                   deltat = double(0),

                   sigma = double(0, default = 1),

                   alpha = double(0, default = 1),

        log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
        returnType(double(0))

        logProb <- -(1/2)*log(2*pi*deltat) - ((deltat*(-2*alpha + sigma^2) + 2*log(x) - 2*log(X0))^2)/(8*deltat*sigma^2)-log(x*sigma)

        if(log) return(logProb)
        else return(exp(logProb))
    })

rsde <- nimbleFunction(

    run = function(n = integer(0),

                   X0 = double(0, default = 0),
                   deltat = double(0),

                   sigma = double(0, default = 1),

                   alpha = double(0, default = 1)) {
        stop('rsde should never be run')

        returnType(double(0))
        return(0)
    })

code <- nimbleCode({

  a0 ~ dnorm(0,sd=1000)
  alpha_mu ~ dunif(0,1)
  alpha_sigma ~ dunif(0,1)
  sigma1 ~ dunif(0,1)

  a1_0 ~ dunif(0,1); # time =11
  a1_1 ~ dsde(X0=a1_0,deltat=1,sigma=alpha_sigma,alpha=alpha_mu)

  Observation[1] ~ dnorm(a0+a1_0*Time[1], sd=sigma1)

})

constants <- list(n = nrow(data1))
data <- list(Observation = data1$Observation)

inits <- list(a0=0.1, sigma1 = 0.01, alpha_sigma=0.01,alpha_mu=0.01,
              a1_0=0.01,
              a1_1=0.1)

model <- nimbleModel(code, constants = constants, data = data1, inits = inits) # build model

myMCMC<-buildMCMC(myMCMCconf)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model,resetFunctions = TRUE)
CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(myMCMC, project = Cmodel,resetFunctions = TRUE)
MCMCsamples <- runMCMC(CmodelMCMC, niter = 200000,thin=20,nchains=1,setSeed=100,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC = FALSE)

messages.body_plain:
Well, the upshot is it's an easy diagnosis and fix again, and also gives the opportunity to try to explain more about the NIMBLE system.  Increase user knowledge base, and ability to trouble-shoot.

Briefly to the point: it's actually *because* you did a simplified example, with "no data likelihood" as you put it, that this is happening.  Now, indeed, I do see that you have "data" in the model, the "Observation" variable.  But, the issue here, is that the "dsde"-distributed parameter, which is "a1_1", itself has no data nodes depending on it.  More technically, the power of MCMC methods is to sample from the *posterioer* distribution of interest, p(parameters | data).  In this case, one dimension of that joint posterior distribution is p(a1_1 | data).  The most common method, Metropolis-Hastings (in NIMBLE, called the RW (random walk)) sampler provides a way - a stochastic accept/reject method - to sample from p(a1_1 | data).  That's pretty amazing!  That's why (and how) modern MCMC is possible, methods like Metropolis-Hasting sampling, which provide a way to handle an (otherwise) very difficult problem.

Now, your case is different.  There's no "data" that depends on "a1_1".  So, fo that node, sampling from p(a1_1 | data), that dimension of the posterior distribution, is the same as sampling from p(a1_1), the prior distribution, since there's no "data" that depends on a1_1.  So, once again, we (nimble) do something that we think is clever, in this case, rather than fussing with stochastic sampling methods, we just sample straight from the prior, because when there's no data, posterior = prior.  So, the simple strategy for generating samples from p(a1_1 | data) = p(a1_1) is to sample from "rsde", the random generation function for the prior distribution.  That's what's causing your problem, and why rsde is being call here.  If there was any "data" that depended on a1_1, then this wouldn't happen.

Within the past year or two, I added a much more concise summary of the sampling algorithms assigned to each node.  Far more concise than the old, original, myMCMCconf$printSamplers() output, which gives a very lengthy output for large models.  The new, concise version:

myMCMCconf$printSamplers(byType = TRUE)

I thought was so insightful, that I (pretty recently) made it print this *by default* when you call configureMCMC().  That's what you're seeing here, below.  Why I point this out, is the existence of a "poserior_predictive" sampler on a1_1 is exactly what we're talking about.  This is a posterior predictive node (has no data depending on it), so this sampler, the posterior_predictive sampler, simply samples from the prior.

> myMCMCconf <- configureMCMC(model)
===== Monitors =====

thin = 1: a0, alpha_mu, alpha_sigma, sigma1, a1_0

===== Samplers =====
RW sampler (4)

  - alpha_mu
  - alpha_sigma
  - sigma1
  - a1_0
posterior_predictive sampler (1)
  - a1_1
conjugate sampler (1)
  - a0

Once you make the change, and add data depending on a1_1, then it will get assigned a RW sampler, instead.

Another option, would be to modify the myMCMCconf configuration object before calling buildMCMC - a powerful functionality that's only really provided by NIMBLE, to customize your own MCMC, and quite easily so - to remove that posterior_predictive sampler, and instead add a RW sampler, which will also work fine:

myMCMCconf$removeSamplers("a1_1")
myMCMCconf$addSampler(target = "a1_1", type = "RW")

Easy peasy.

You have multiple possible paths forward here.

Keep at it.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
thanks Daniel, yes easy peasy :-) As a suggestion I do wonder if
perhaps it's worth noting this somewhere in the documentation for
those coming from JAGS etc - ok, if you get into the details of the
nimble sampler documentation then it's obvious that this problem will
occur - but for the lazy bones out there who don't RTFM and are used
to JAGS/BUGS then this is quite subtle and different behaviour from
JAGS (at least I've never had this issue in JAGS, which in this case I
guess would just choose a slice sampler and problem solved). I know
it's the price of the flexibility you've built into nimble! thanks
again for another speed solution. Fraser.

More technically, the power of MCMC methods is to sample from the *posterioer* distribution of interest, p(parameters | data).  In this case, one dimension of that joint posterior distribution is p(a1_1 | data).  The most common method, Metropolis-Hastings (in NIMBLE, called the RW (random walk)) sampler provides a way - a stochastic accept/reject method - to sample from p(a1_1 | data).  That's pretty amazing!  That's why (and how) modern MCMC is possible, methods like Metropolis-Hasting sampling, which provide a way to handle an (otherwise) very difficult problem.
>
> Now, your case is different.  There's no "data" that depends on "a1_1".  So, fo that node, sampling from p(a1_1 | data), that dimension of the posterior distribution, is the same as sampling from p(a1_1), the prior distribution, since there's no "data" that depends on a1_1.  So, once again, we (nimble) do something that we think is clever, in this case, rather than fussing with stochastic sampling methods, we just sample straight from the prior, because when there's no data, posterior = prior.  So, the simple strategy for generating samples from p(a1_1 | data) = p(a1_1) is to sample from "rsde", the random generation function for the prior distribution.  That's what's causing your problem, and why rsde is being call here.  If there was any "data" that depended on a1_1, then this wouldn't happen.
>
> Within the past year or two, I added a much more concise summary of the sampling algorithms assigned to each node.  Far more concise than the old, original, myMCMCconf$printSamplers() output, which gives a very lengthy output for large models.  The new, concise version:
>
> myMCMCconf$printSamplers(byType = TRUE)
>
> I thought was so insightful, that I (pretty recently) made it print this *by default* when you call configureMCMC().  That's what you're seeing here, below.  Why I point this out, is the existence of a "poserior_predictive" sampler on a1_1 is exactly what we're talking about.  This is a posterior predictive node (has no data depending on it), so this sampler, the posterior_predictive sampler, simply samples from the prior.
>
> > myMCMCconf <- configureMCMC(model)
> ===== Monitors =====
> thin = 1: a0, alpha_mu, alpha_sigma, sigma1, a1_0
> ===== Samplers =====
> RW sampler (4)
>   - alpha_mu
>   - alpha_sigma
>   - sigma1
>   - a1_0
> posterior_predictive sampler (1)
>   - a1_1
> conjugate sampler (1)
>   - a0
>
> Once you make the change, and add data depending on a1_1, then it will get assigned a RW sampler, instead.
>
> Another option, would be to modify the myMCMCconf configuration object before calling buildMCMC - a powerful functionality that's only really provided by NIMBLE, to customize your own MCMC, and quite easily so - to remove that posterior_predictive sampler, and instead add a RW sampler, which will also work fine:
>
> myMCMCconf$removeSamplers("a1_1")
> myMCMCconf$addSampler(target = "a1_1", type = "RW")
>
> Easy peasy.
>
> You have multiple possible paths forward here.
>
> Keep at it.
>
> Daniel
